items.snippet: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. items.title: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks
items.snippet: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks, raising intriguing questions about the Red Planet's potential to have supported life. The remarkable preservation of these compounds, along with similar discoveries thousands of miles away, suggests the building blocks of life may once have been widespread across Mars.

items.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
items.snippet: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.

items.title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
items.snippet: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.

items.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
items.snippet: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.

items.title: Children are not colorblind: Why early conversations about race are essential
items.snippet: Discussing racism with children can seem daunting to parents, caregivers and educators for several reasons. Often, it can feel uncomfortable talking about people's differences; conversations about racism reveal implicit biases and, for some, immense privilege.

items.title: Research advances quantum computing that harnesses speed of light
items.snippet: Quantum computers have the potential to perform calculations more quickly than supercomputers, but they could be even faster and more energy-efficient if they were built with photons as their basic units, called qubits.

items.title: Automated assembly in space is the future and NOM4D is showing the way
items.snippet: If we want big things in space, we'll have to build and assemble them there. Rocket fairings are not large enough to accommodate the large things we want to have in space. Not only that, but the stubborn rocket equation refuses to bend itself to our desires.

items.title: Trusted online information may help networking skills translate into startup ambitions, survey suggests
items.snippet: A study of almost 200 undergraduate and postgraduate students in South Korea suggests that the skills of aspiring entrepreneurs are more likely to translate into plans to start a business when supported by trustworthy digital networks and useful online resources. Details of the findings are reported in the World Review of Entrepreneurship, Management and Sustainable Development.

items.title: Not afraid of ghosts: Curiosity and fearlessness apparent in German shepherd genes
items.snippet: German shepherd dogs bred for working are more curious and less neurotic than German shepherds bred for show. A new study from Uppsala University and the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences has shown that the differences are not only apparent in the dogs' behavior, but also in their genes. items.title: Global climate policies continue to advance despite setbacks, research finds
items.snippet: The latest findings from the Oxford Climate Policy Monitor, led by the Blavatnik School of Government and the Oxford Sustainable Law Programme, show that progress in Asia, Africa and Latin America is more than offsetting the weakening or reversal of climate policies in parts of Europe and North America.

items.title: Product for controlling agricultural pests proves harmful to iconic banana slug
items.snippet: Researchers at Oregon State University say a product used to control pest slugs on farms in multiple countries is harmful to an iconic West Coast slug and that more research is needed before the product is approved for use in the United States. The work is published in the journal PLOS One.

items.snippet: When it comes to making decisions regarding mortgage foreclosures, a bank doesn't know what it doesn't know.

items.title: Astronomy is the universe looking back at itself
items.snippet: When you see the sun, you’re seeing it as it was eight minutes ago, and the faintest star yet observed, Earendel, shines from 12.9 billion years in the past. Astronomer Michelle Thaller, who spent 28 years at NASA, explains how every telescope is a time machine and how gravity itself bends space into natural lenses that let us peer to the dawn of the universe.
